finding: This round replaced the withdrawn sink-validation mechanism with a normative PRECONDITION on the release's own default, and then ships the default anyway, so §2 asserts both sides of the same gate. Line 88-93: 'before `blocking` may gate, the severity a row carries must be checkable by something other than the row's author, and the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition. Four incompatible answers to the second exist and this section picks none of them ... which is why §7 has no test for it yet.' Line 111 then reads 'Default. `blocking`'. So the release ships as its default the exact behaviour it has just declared may not gate until two conditions it does not meet are met. Worse, §2 also asserts the FIRST condition is already satisfied: line 105-107 says `severity` 'is checkable against the finding's own text by a later round, which is what every round of this cycle has been doing to the round before it' -- present tense, no mechanism needed. Two engineers therefore write opposite tests and both cite §2: one asserts `blocking` is refused (or warns) until a checker exists, the other asserts nothing at all because the condition is met by construction. Neither can be falsified, because the 'four incompatible answers' are never enumerated -- a decomposer cannot pick one and a tester cannot name the observable that separates them.
suggestion: Pick one of three and say which: (a) the precondition is met by later-round review, in which case delete 'before blocking may gate' and keep only the §2.1 measurement as the argument; (b) the precondition is not met, in which case the default must be `all` in THIS release with `blocking` opt-in, and §7 gains a test that the shipped default is `all`; (c) the precondition is real and unmet and the field does not ship. Whichever is chosen, enumerate the four answers for the 67 rows with the one selected marked, or move that whole question to a named later release and drop it from this release's requirements -- an unenumerated 'four answers, none picked' is not a requirement a task can be written against.

finding: This round replaced §2's withdrawn sink-validation mechanism with a precondition I cannot satisfy inside this release, while the same section still ships the behaviour the precondition gates. §2 now states: "before `blocking` may gate, the severity a row carries must be checkable by something other than the row's author, and the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition", and then says the section "picks none" of the four answers to the second half. The only checker §2 offers for the first half is prose: severity "is checkable against the finding's own text by a later round" -- a later agent, not an artifact, so nothing in a task's acceptance can assert it. The one mechanical checker that was on the table is now fenced out by the tightened Non-Goal 3: "Any future proposal that makes `--record` refuse a row is a different release, and this one must gate on what is already recorded or not gate at all." Meanwhile §2's Default paragraph ships `blocking`, and §7 test 1 pins default `blocking` as acceptance. So the release simultaneously forbids `blocking` from gating until a condition is met, forecloses the only stated way to meet it, and requires a test asserting `blocking` is the default. Building this means picking one of the three by myself, and each pick changes what ships.
suggestion: Resolve the precondition against the default in one clause. Either (a) ship `all` as the default for this release and state that `blocking` becomes the default once the checkability requirement is discharged in a named later release, so §7 test 1 pins `all`; or (b) drop the word precondition -- state that `blocking` gates on the severity as recorded, with the self-declared-label risk accepted and named, and delete "before `blocking` may gate"; or (c) keep the precondition and name the artifact that discharges it inside this release, with a §7 test. Whichever is chosen, say explicitly whether the 67 recorded rows block `blocking` from being usable on this repository today.

finding: §2 now states a normative precondition for the release's own default and then ships the default without meeting it, in the same section. The precondition: 'before `blocking` may gate, the severity a row carries must be *checkable by something other than the row's author*, and the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition.' The same paragraph then says 'Four incompatible answers to the second exist and this section picks none of them, which is the honest state and is why §7 has no test for it yet.' Four paragraphs later: 'Default. `blocking`, matching `review_converge_on`.' Read together the release says: blocking may not gate until X; X is undecided and untested; blocking is the default. This is not the round-1/round-2 defect (a false validation claim, then a withdrawn validation mechanism) — those were about whether an argument was true. This is structural: with the mechanism withdrawn, the section's own gate condition is now an unmet obligation sitting above the clause it gates, and nothing in §5, §6 or §7 records that the default is conditional or that the condition is open. A decomposer reading §2 cannot write acceptance for the default, because §2 forbids shipping it.
suggestion: Pick one and say it plainly: (a) default `all` for this release, with `blocking` opt-in, and the precondition named as what a later release must satisfy before the default can flip — this is the only reading under which the release ships nothing it has forbidden; or (b) withdraw the precondition sentence and state instead that the release gates on a self-declared, unvalidated label and accepts that risk, with the 67 rows' disposition stated as a Non-Goal with its reason. Either way §7 needs a test that pins which of the two shipped.

finding: The `--check` requirement this round took back from `spec/0.46.0.md` §8 arrives as one sentence and nothing else, and that sentence makes a false statement about this document. §2.0a: "**It takes it back:** `--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`, and §7 gains the test that pins them equal." §7 holds eight tests and none of them names `--check`, `--status`, or a parity assertion -- tests 1-4 are the field and the replay, 5 is the disposition, 6-8 are the reset. So the section that adds the requirement asserts its own acceptance exists when it does not. Three further pieces I would have to invent to build it: (1) placement -- `converged` on both surfaces comes from `engine.Converged(rounds, required, hash)` (`audit_record.go:95` for --record, `:333` for --status/--check), which folds the streak internally, so "reads the same predicate" needs a statement of where the severity predicate enters that fold; (2) exit code -- `--status --check` is an exit-code gate, and the release never says what it exits when `blocking` is satisfied but non-blocking rows survive; (3) the surfacing half -- §2.0a itself records that `nonblocking_open` is review-only and that surfacing the remaining rows "means creating an audit-side counterpart, which this release must declare and test rather than assume -- §7 does not", and taking the requirement back did not add that declaration. §5 compounds this: it still lists "the `--check` divergence" among the three sections exported to `spec/0.46.0.md` and closes "This release is §2, §3 and §4", so a decomposer reading §5 will not create a `--check` task at all.
suggestion: Add the §7 test the sentence claims -- e.g. "a state in which `--record` counts a round clean under `blocking` is reported converged by `--status --check` at the same audit_clean_rounds, and the two disagree under `all`" -- and state its exit code. Name the audit-side counterpart to `nonblocking_open` (key, value, which surfaces carry it) or say plainly that surviving non-blocking rows are surfaced by an existing key. Amend §5 so the `--check` half is no longer listed as exported, or the takeback and the removal notice will decompose into different releases.

finding: The take-back buys surface and closes nothing, and this spec supplies the proof. §2.0a says the release "either takes the --check half back or states plainly that it does not close the gap it opens with" and then "It takes it back: --check reads the same predicate as --record". The gap it claims to close is spec/0.46.0.md §8, and §8's diagnosis is role scoping, not severity: "consecutive_clean counts rounds with zero findings across every role" while the shipping rule reads spec_coverage_clean_rounds plus no-FAIL, and §8's own two candidate shapes are converge_roles and a conformance-streak predicate -- neither of which is severity parity. §8 has already been edited to cede the requirement ("which spec/0.37.0.md §2.0a has since taken back into that release"), so no other release now carries it. On the very cycle §8 was written about, parity leaves --check where it was: §2.0a itself records that v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13 produced error-severity findings, error is blocking, so a parity --check at that cycle's stop still exits 1 -- which is exactly the "never -- no round reaches zero" cell §2.1 gives that cycle. The release therefore adds a --check obligation and a parity test to close a gap it does not touch, and the only release that could have closed it has been emptied.
suggestion: Take back what §8 actually asked for, or take nothing back. If parity is the intent, say plainly that it makes --record and --check agree and does NOT reach §8's role-scoping gap, and restore that requirement to spec/0.46.0.md §8 instead of leaving it owned by a release that cannot satisfy it. Either way, state the v0.36.0 outcome under parity (still exit 1) beside the claim, since the release already has that measurement.

finding: The take-back paragraph 17d3007 added ends: 'It takes it back: --check reads the same predicate as --record, and §7 GAINS THE TEST that pins them equal.' §7 gained nothing. Verified with `git diff 9864b00 HEAD -- spec/0.37.0.md`: neither f9295e2 nor 17d3007 touched §7, and the eight test lines are byte-identical to the round-1 and round-2 snapshots. suggestion: Add the test to §7: under blocking, a round whose only surviving non-PASS rows are warning/info makes `tp audit --status --check` exit 0, and the same round under all exits 1; and a round carrying one error row exits 1 under both. Until that line exists in §7, change §2.0a to state the requirement ('§7 must gain a test that pins them equal') rather than reporting it as done.

finding: §2.0a makes a present-tense factual claim about this spec's own contents that is false: '`--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`, and §7 gains the test that pins them equal.' §7 holds eight tests and none of them mentions `--check`, `--status`, or parity between the two surfaces: 1 precedence + illegal literal, 2 blocking vs all on one round, 3 one error keeps the round dirty, 4 the v0.35.0 nine-round replay, 5 disposition exclusion, 6 spec_hash reset, 7 reset preserves recorded rounds, 8 unchanged spec records an identical streak. The same section states a second obligation on §7 and marks it unmet in the same sentence — 'surfacing the remaining rows means creating an audit-side counterpart, which this release must declare and test rather than assume — §7 does not.' So §2.0a contains one 'must ... §7 does not' that is honest and one 'and §7 gains the test' that is not, two paragraphs apart, and a reader has no way to tell which of the section's other assertions about the release are descriptions and which are intentions. This is distinct from the standing 'untested normative section' findings: it is not that a clause lacks a test, it is that the spec asserts the test exists.
suggestion: Write the two tests, or write neither and say so in the same words §2.0a already uses for the other gap. If they are written: (9) `--status --check` and `--record` return the same clean/dirty verdict for the same round under each `audit_converge_on` value; (10) a clean round with surviving non-blocking audit rows emits the audit-side counterpart field, named here and added to skills/tp/REFERENCE.md's --compact list, superseding spec/0.31.0.md §8.4's 'never an audit field'.

finding: §2.0a takes the `--check` requirement back from spec/0.46.0.md §8 and closes it with one mechanism — 'It takes it back: `--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`' — and that mechanism does not satisfy the acceptance test §8 states for the requirement, on the cycle both specs cite. §8's test: 'a fixture where the conformance role is clean for `required_clean_rounds` running while another role has open non-FAIL rows must reach exit 0, and must not reach it if the conformance role has an open row.' Measured on spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/: rounds 12 and 13 carry 2 `error` rows each, and every one belongs to `maintainability-conventions` (r12: 2 PARTIAL/error; r13: 2 FAIL/error + 1 PARTIAL/warning) while `spec-coverage` was clean for four consecutive rounds. Under `audit_converge_on=blocking` an `error` row blocks, so predicate parity leaves `--check` at exit 1 for exactly the rounds §8 says must reach exit 0. §8 also names two candidate shapes for the requirement — a role-scoped convergence set (`converge_roles`) or a `--check` reporting the shipping predicate — and says neither is chosen; §2.0a's mechanism is neither of them, and §2.0a never says it is replacing them. So the release claims to close a gap with a mechanism that is untested here, unnamed there, and falsified by the measurement both sections share. §2.0a's own 'One caveat' paragraph concedes the same data (v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13 produced two error findings 'invisible to the conformance role') without noticing that it refutes the take-back three paragraphs above it.
suggestion: Either drop the take-back and state plainly that `audit_converge_on` changes what `--record` reports and nothing about the command `tp run` gates on (the honest branch §2.0a itself offers), leaving §8 whole in spec/0.46.0.md; or take back the requirement WITH one of §8's two candidate mechanisms, state which, and add §8's fixture as a §7 test — the v0.36.0 r10-r13 shape is a ready-made fixture and this release would fail it as written.

finding: §2.0a's closing sentence (line 150-151) is the only place this release takes back the --check half, and it makes a false claim about its own document plus an untestable one about the code: 'It takes it back: `--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`, and §7 gains the test that pins them equal.' §7 is byte-identical to round 1 -- eight tests, none of them about --check -- so 'gains' names a test that does not exist, and the clause that makes the release shippable (§2.0a line 145-150: without it, blocking 'changes nothing about the command an operator or `tp run` actually gates on') has no acceptance. The deeper defect is that the obvious form of the promised test passes against UNMODIFIED tp today and therefore cannot fail for the reason the clause exists: `--record` computes consecutive_clean at audit_record.go:101 and `--status`/`--check` at audit_record.go:339, and both are `engine.ConsecutiveClean(rounds)` over the SAME stored `Clean` booleans (stamped once at audit_record.go:71 as `findings == 0`). An equality assertion over those two payloads is green before a line of this release is written. And 'the same predicate' silently decides a fork §3 declares OPEN: §3 line 214-218 says 'Either audit's clean flag is recomputed live from rows ... or the disposition has to survive into the next round's input -- and this release has to pick one'. --check reading the same predicate as --record is only implementable under live recomputation, so §2.0a picks the fork §3 says is unpicked, in the same release, without saying so.
suggestion: State the mechanism, then state the test with the fixture that makes it discriminate. Mechanism: audit's --status must recompute each round's clean flag live from its recorded rows under the resolved audit_converge_on before calling ConsecutiveClean/Converged -- the shipped review twin does exactly this and is the citation §2.0a is missing (review_status.go:57-65 overwrites rounds[i].Clean with engine.ReviewRoundClean, and its comment gives the reason: it 'lets switching the setting or resolving a finding re-evaluate a round without re-recording'). Test: record round 1 and round 2 under audit_converge_on=all from a results file whose only non-PASS rows are severity `warning`, so both rounds store clean:false and --status --check exits 1; then `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` and, WITHOUT recording anything, assert (i) `tp audit spec.md --status` reports consecutive_clean 2 and converged true, (ii) `tp audit spec.md --status --check` exits 0, and (iii) those values equal what a `--record` re-run of the same file reports. Then flip back to `all` and assert all three revert. A stored-flag implementation fails (i)-(iii) and passes the trivial equality, which is what separates the two designs. Add the mirror case -- one `error` row -- so the test cannot pass by ignoring severity entirely.

finding: The §4 repair answered round 2's derived-value findings (ax-economist store-what-could-be-derived, implementer reset-of-a-derived-value) by rewriting the mechanism from a record-time reset to an output-time truncation, and in doing so added one clause that falsifies §2.1's table and §7 test 4 -- the release's entire quantitative case. The old text was prospective: 'When tp audit --record sees a spec_hash different from the previous round's, it resets consecutive_clean to zero.' The new text is 'stop that walk at the first spec_hash boundary -- zero stored bytes, idempotent under RecordRound's rewrite path, and RETROACTIVE OVER ROUNDS ALREADY ON DISK'. Measured against the exact corpus §2.1 and test 4 name -- spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json plus audit-round-1..9.ndjson -- the nine recorded v0.35.0 rounds carry eight distinct spec_hash values (r1=r2 a46f45c6, r3 c06544ea, r4 50be1428, r5 2dd780c6, r6 6f42a8eb, r7=r8 1259a4af, r9 54e031e6). Simulating both predicates with audit_clean_rounds:2: today blocking converges at round 3 and all at round 9, which is what §2.1's row and test 4 assert. With §4's retroactive truncation applied, blocking converges at round 8 and all NEVER converges -- the only two clean rounds, r8 and r9, are separated by a spec_hash boundary, so the streak the `all` cell depends on cannot exist. So this release contains a section whose mechanism, applied to this release's own replay fixture, changes 'round 3 / round 9' to 'round 8 / never'. That destroys the headline economic claim too: 'six rounds of a nine-round phase spent on a population that was 93% advisory' becomes one round saved. Nothing in the spec says the replay runs with §4 disabled, and §7 test 4 says the replay 'reproduces the recorded history exactly', which under the shipped pair it does not.
suggestion: Either drop 'retroactive over rounds already on disk' and keep §4 prospective (the pre-repair form, which is what makes §2.1 and test 4 true), or keep retroactivity and re-measure §2.1's whole table under the composed rule and rewrite test 4's expected values. If test 4 is deliberately a §2-only replay with §4 switched off, say so in test 4 and drop 'reproducing the recorded history exactly', because the shipped binary will not reproduce it. Add a §7 test that composes the two sections, since the composition is where the release contradicts itself.

finding: §4 now picks an implementation site -- "the reset is applied by the audit caller ... The audit-caller form is the one that composes" -- and that pick cannot reach the value the release gates on. The two call sites §4 cites (`audit_record.go:101`, `:339`) are the two places `consecutive_clean` is printed. The value that decides anything is `converged`, and it is not computed from those calls: `engine.Converged(rounds, requiredCleanRounds, currentHash)` (`engine/reviewstate.go:510`) calls `ConsecutiveClean` inside itself, and audit reaches it at `audit_record.go:95` (--record) and `audit_record.go:333` (--status/--check), with `cli/run_status.go:149` and `cli/budget.go:26` reading it for the run driver and the budget signal. An audit caller cannot make that fold hash-aware without a new engine entry point, and §4 names none; Non-Goal 4 forbids changing the shared one because `review_status.go:67` calls the same function. Built as §4 now specifies it, the reset changes two printed integers while `converged`, `budget_exhausted`, `tp resume` and `tp run`'s oracle keep the pre-reset answer -- and §2.0a in this same round made `--check`, which reads exactly that `converged`, a requirement of this release. §4 also states the collision only against `review_status.go:91`, which is the printed integer, not `:67`, which is the predicate.
suggestion: Name the function this release adds -- e.g. `engine.AuditConsecutiveClean(rounds)` (hash-aware trailing walk) and `engine.AuditConverged(rounds, required, currentHash)` -- and list every audit call site that must switch to them: `audit_record.go:95`, `:101`, `:333`, `:339`, `audit.go:352`, plus the audit branches of `run_status.go:149` and `budget.go:26`. State that `engine.ConsecutiveClean` and `engine.Converged` keep their current semantics for review, which is the form that actually satisfies Non-Goal 4. Then add a §7 test asserting `converged`, not just `consecutive_clean`, changes across a spec_hash boundary.

finding: Taken as a whole the release is not decomposable at the boundary §5 draws, and the reason is not any single defect: two of its three sections now END on an undischarged decision, and that is a stable property rather than a repairable sentence. §2: 'before `blocking` may gate ... the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition. Four incompatible answers to the second exist and this section picks none of them.' §3: 'Either audit's clean flag is recomputed live from rows ... or the disposition has to survive into the next round's input — and this release has to pick one', and it does not; §3 also records a second unfixed blocker in its own mechanism — dedupAuditRows (audit_merge.go:191-203, verified: keeps the first (role,item_id) row and compares nothing, where review's merge keeps the highest severity) means that under `blocking` the order role files are passed to --merge decides whether a round is clean — which §6 does not defer and §7 does not test, so the release's central default is nondeterministic by its own account. §4 is the only section with a decided mechanism (stop engine.ConsecutiveClean's walk at the first spec_hash boundary, applied by the audit caller so review is untouched). §5 asserts 'a release whose remainder (§2, §3, §4) has mechanisms and tests today' — that is true only of §4. What §2 and §3 have today is a diagnosis each, written by the round that refuted the previous mechanism, plus an instruction to a later reader to choose. Section length is being driven by narration of withdrawn drafts rather than by mechanism: the removal of ~100 lines in §5 left the file at 306 lines, longer than the 288 it was removing from. The pattern across three rounds is that §2 produces a mechanism, the next round refutes it, and the refutation is added to §2 — so §2 grows monotonically and its decided content does not.
suggestion: Ship the honest smaller release: §4 alone, plus `audit_converge_on` as a resolved, documented, tested field whose DEFAULT is `all` — that is pure plumbing, changes no recorded outcome, and is what §2.1's own measurement supports ('`all` reproduces the recorded history exactly'). Move to a later release, together because they are one problem: the default flip to `blocking`, the sink question and the 67 rows' disposition (§2), the live-recomputation-vs-persisted-disposition choice and the merge-order fix (§3), and the `--check` half (§2.0a / spec/0.46.0.md §8). That release can be written once the three choices are made, and each is a decision a person makes in minutes — none of them needs another review round to discover. Keeping them here costs rounds precisely because a review round cannot make a choice; it can only observe that none was made, which is what rounds 1, 2 and 3 have each done.

finding: Two sections of this release give different answers to what the release contains, and a third file agrees with only one of them. §5 closes: 'They are `spec/0.46.0.md` §8, §8a and §8b ... This release is §2, §3 and §4.' §2.0a says the opposite for §8: '**It takes it back:** `--check` reads the same predicate as `--record`, and §7 gains the test that pins them equal.' spec/0.46.0.md §8 has already been edited to match §2.0a — 'the same distinction has to reach `--check` — **which `spec/0.37.0.md` §2.0a has since taken back into that release** ... What remains here is the observation and its measurement, not the requirement.' So the sibling spec has handed the requirement over, §2.0a has accepted it, and §5 still lists it as departed. §1 counts the same scope a third way — 'This release gives audit the two things review already has' — which covers §2 and §4 but not §3's disposition rule and not §2.0a's `--check` half. Three enumerations of one release, no two alike, in a spec whose §5 exists specifically to state the boundary. The failure mode is concrete rather than editorial: a decomposer following §5 writes no task for `--check`, and spec/0.46.0.md no longer carries one either, so the requirement lands in no release — which is the exact defect §2.0a says it is fixing.
suggestion: Make §5 the single statement of scope and reconcile the other two to it. If the take-back stands, §5 must read 'This release is §2, §2.0a's `--check` half, §3 and §4; §8a and §8b are spec/0.46.0.md', §1's 'two things' becomes three or four, and §7 gains the tests §2.0a promises. If it does not stand, delete the take-back sentence from §2.0a and revert spec/0.46.0.md §8's inserted clause in the same change, so the two files do not disagree about who owns the requirement.

finding: Non-Goal 3 says this release "only reads" severity, but there is nothing that reads the audit vocabulary, and the one shipped reader inverts it. engine.SeverityRank (internal/engine/cluster.go:32-41) maps critical 0, high 1, medium 2, low 3 and returns 4 for everything else, so error, warning and info all rank 4 -- §2's own table says this. The 67 legacy rows §2 counts carry high/medium/low, which that map DOES rank. So the cheap path -- reuse the shipped ranker, as review's merge does at review_merge.go:224 -- orders a legacy low (3) as more severe than a current error (4), and a blocking set written as SeverityRank(s) <= SeverityRank("high") makes every error row non-blocking and every legacy low row blocking. The release needs an audit-vocabulary rank or blocking set in at least two places: §2's clean predicate, and §3's merge fix ("where review's merge keeps the highest severity" -- that comparison does not exist for audit and cannot be added without one). Neither the function, its unknown-value behaviour, nor a test for it appears in §7, so decomposition either invents it twice or discovers the dependency mid-implementation.
suggestion: Name the audit blocking set explicitly in §2 (which of error|warning|info blocks, and what an unrecognised or legacy value does) as a predicate over the audit vocabulary, and state that engine.SeverityRank is the REVIEW ranker and must not be reused. Add one §7 test pinning error blocking, warning/info not, and a legacy high/medium/low row resolving the way §2 says -- otherwise the merge fix in §3 has no comparator to call.

finding: The bolded lead-in 'The field it reads exists and is NOT validated, and **this release's first job is to fix that**' is falsified by the two paragraphs under it and by §6. §2 goes on to withdraw the fix ('the first attempt at building it was withdrawn in the round after it was written', four numbered refutations), replaces it with a requirement it explicitly does not answer, and Non-Goal 3 closes the door: 'Any future proposal that makes `--record` refuse a row is a different release, and this one must gate on what is already recorded or not gate at all.' So the release's stated first job is, by its own Non-Goal, not in the release. The heading survives because the round-2 repair rewrote the paragraph body and left its bolded claim in place — the same shape as the round-1 repair that left a false claim in the opening sentence while correcting the table beneath it. Bolded lead-ins in this section are being read as summaries and are drifting from the text they summarise faster than the text changes.
suggestion: Change the lead-in to what the section now does: 'The field it reads exists and is NOT validated, and this release gates on it anyway' — or, if that is not acceptable, do not ship the gate. Then re-read every other bolded lead-in in §2 against its own paragraph; at least three now describe a draft that no longer exists.

finding: The precondition spends the exact resource the knob exists to save, and Non-Goal 3 has now closed the cheap way to meet it. §2 requires that "before blocking may gate, the severity a row carries must be checkable by something other than the row's author". Non-Goal 3 forecloses the sink ("Any future proposal that makes --record refuse a row is a different release, and this one must gate on what is already recorded or not gate at all"), so the only checker §2 leaves is the one it names itself: severity "is checkable against the finding's own text by a later round". A later audit round is one merged file times every role in the corpus -- under tp run, one subagent process each -- which is the most expensive round-trip tp has. The knob's whole measured value is rounds: §2.1 scores it saving six of nine on v0.35.0. So a gate that must be checked by a round can save at most (rounds saved minus one) and, on the two-clean-rounds rule, must be checked in each round it wants to end. The release ships with the precondition unmet either way: state it and the gate never arms, drop it and blocking gates on a label the release just spent forty lines proving nothing checks.
suggestion: Price the precondition before adopting it. If the only checker is a later round, say what the gate costs in rounds and compare it against §2.1's six-round saving -- that comparison is the release's actual AX case and it is not made anywhere. If the arithmetic does not survive, the honest options are defaulting to all (zero migration, zero new decision for every existing project) or dropping the precondition and stating that blocking gates on an unchecked self-declared label, which is the same objection §2 uses to defer scope a fourth time.

finding: The requirement added this round uses the word "disposition" for something other than the `disposition` §3 defines two sections later, and the two readings produce opposite code. §2: "the 67 recorded rows must have a stated disposition" -- in context this means a decision about what to do with out-of-enum severities (migrate, ignore, treat as blocking, treat as advisory). §3: "A row carrying a `wontfix` or `duplicate` disposition is excluded from the round's finding count", i.e. a per-row stored key with a fixed vocabulary and an exclusion rule. An implementer decomposing §2 can discharge its requirement literally -- stamp a disposition on those 67 rows -- which under §3's rule silently excludes fifteen rounds of recorded findings from every count that reads them, and would look like compliance with both sections. Nothing in either section says the two words are different things.

finding: Non-Goal 3's new closing clause and §2's new requirement are mutually exclusive, and neither names the other. finding: Test 6 still requires an output key the new §4 mechanism has no event for. §4 was rewritten this round into the derived form -- the streak walk stops at the first spec_hash boundary, "zero stored bytes", nothing mutates -- and test 6's second clause survives from the withdrawn stored-reset draft: "resets consecutive_clean to zero AND reports the reset on the machine-readable surface". finding: §4 identifies, in this round's own text, the one way this release can silently break another phase -- and §7 contains no test that would catch it, so the broken implementation passes the whole list. §4 lines 243-246: '`engine.ConsecutiveClean` is shared with review's `--status` (`review_status.go:91`). finding: §2.0a's take-back states a parity as settled that §3, in the same commit, states cannot be settled yet. §2.0a: 'It takes it back: --check reads the same predicate as --record.' §3: 'clean is stamped at record time (audit_record.go:71, :208) and ConsecutiveClean walks the STORED FLAGS, while --resolve writes the disposition into the round file afterwards ... Either audit's clean flag is recomputed LIVE from rows, the way review's twin already does (review_status.go:91), or the disposition has to survive into the next round's input -- and THIS RELEASE HAS TO PICK ONE.' It picks neither. But --record stamps a flag and --status/--check reads flags, so whether the two commands can read 'the same predicate' at all is precisely the stored-versus-live question §3 leaves open: under the stored form they cannot (a --check run after audit_converge_on changes, or after a --resolve, reads a flag computed under the old rule), and under the live form they can. §4 then makes it three-way, because its truncation is stated as a change to the ConsecutiveClean walk -- the stored-flag reader. So three sections of this release depend on one decision, each describes it differently, and none makes it. Round 2's implementer (stored-vs-live-clean-predicate, critical) and ax-economist (cached-verdict-vs-live-predicate, high) both filed against this; the repair recorded the problem in §3 and then wrote a new dependency on the unmade decision into §2.0a.

finding: §3 correctly records that under blocking the order role files reach --merge decides whether a round is clean, and stops one step short of the cost: the agent cannot recover the decision from tp's own output. dedupAuditRows (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:191-211) drops the later row silently and then sorts the survivors by (role, item_id), so the merged file no longer carries the input order that decided the verdict, and --merge reports only duplicates_removed as a bare count (audit_merge.go:59) -- no ids, no roles, no severities. finding: Test 4 hard-codes two numbers against a corpus nothing in the repository pins, and its own defence of runnability answers a different objection than the one that applies. It reads 'Replayed against this repository's nine recorded v0.35.0 audit rounds, `blocking` converges at round 3 and `all` at round 9 ... The replay reads `status` and `severity` off recorded rows and needs no spec snapshot, which is why it is runnable where `spec/0.43.0.md` §6's corpus gates are not.' The snapshot point is correct and I verified the expectations hold today: spec/.tp-review/0.35.0 has 9 rounds; r2 and r3 carry zero `error` rows (r2 {info 7, warning 5}, r3 {info 3, warning 2}) so `blocking` stops at 3, and r8/r9 are the only fully-PASS rounds so `all` stops at 9. But the test's inputs are live, mutable, committed repository state, not a fixture: any later `tp audit spec/0.35.0.md --record`, any `--resolve` writing a disposition into those round files, and `spec/0.45.0.md` §3's `--reconcile` (which rewrites a round's stored hash) each move the numbers, and the test then fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the predicate under test. That is the failure mode CLAUDE.md's own rule warns about -- a claim bound to a named artifact cannot rot silently, but only if the artifact is pinned -- and it is the same class as the suite-state wrapper's reason for existing: a test whose subject is a spec still sitting in the repository.

finding: NEAR-MISS (not a spec defect; recorded as asked). I drafted a finding that §7 test 7 ('The reset does not delete or rewrite any recorded round') is unfalsifiable, on §4's own words: 'zero stored bytes ... which makes §7 test 7 true by construction rather than by fixture' -- a test the spec advertises as unable to fail, against CLAUDE.md's rule that a test never observed failing proves nothing. suggestion: Before filing a vacuity finding on any test, name the mutation that would kill it; if one exists, the test is a guard and the finding belongs on its neighbours instead.
